idiom_name: std::unordered_map memo keyed by (rule_id << 32 | pos), parser as a class
implementation_notes: The standard library supplies the table and not the pattern: a std::unordered_map<std::uint64_t, Memo> on a packed key (or a small key struct) holds one entry per attempted rule/position pair, and Memo carries both the success (node plus end offset) and the recorded failure, because find() only distinguishes 'not computed'. What replaces the classic memo-table object is one lookup/store pair around each rule member function while the parser class owns the table, so the table dies with the parser. reserve() the map from rules * (input_length + 1) - growing it during the parse is the common performance mistake - and remember that element references and pointers survive rehashing while iterators do not, so an iterator held across a recursive rule call is a latent bug. Choose this hashed form when rule/position pairs are sparse; choose the dense-vector variant when the whole in-memory input is parsed in one pass.
pitfalls: Packing rule id and position into one 64-bit key breaks silently when the input exceeds 2^32 positions or the rule count exceeds 2^16 - use a pair key or assert the bounds.
Iterators into the map are invalidated when an insert rehashes while element references stay valid: never keep an iterator across a recursive rule call, keep the key or a copy instead.
Every boxed key/value pair is a separate allocation and growth rehashes repeatedly; reserve() up front and prefer a small struct key (or the dense variant) in parsers that run hot.

variants.name: Dense per-rule std::vector<std::optional<Memo>> indexed by position
variants.idiom_name: std::vector<std::vector<Memo>> addressed as memo[rule][pos], optional for not-computed
variants.implementation_notes: Because positions are bounded by the input length the memo needs no hashing at all: allocate std::vector<std::vector<Memo>> memo(rules, std::vector<Memo>(len + 1)) and index it as memo[rule][pos], with std::optional (or a three-state enum) separating 'not computed' from 'computed and failed'. What replaces the classic structure is arithmetic indexing: one contiguous row per rule, no key hashing, no per-entry node allocation and better cache behaviour for batch parsing - at the cost of allocating rules x (len + 1) cells up front even where a rule is never tried at most positions. Ford's category split (grouping rules into a few levels) is the middle ground for grammars with many rules.
pitfalls: rules x (len + 1) cells are allocated even for positions a rule never visits; for many-rule grammars the sparse map is smaller (split the table into rule categories, as Ford suggests).

std::vector<std::vector<...>> means one heap allocation per rule and a reallocation of the outer vector can move rows; a flat std::vector<Memo> of size rules*(len+1) with index arithmetic avoids both but gives up independent rows.
